en: The Scripture on the Universal Gate Chapter Spoken by the Buddha, translated by Dharmarakṣa of the Western Jin Dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Vulture Peak Mountain in the city of Rājagṛha, together with a great assembly of...

The assembly of bhikṣus numbered eight hundred, and there were forty-two thousand bodhisattvas—those who had attained all dhāraṇīs, whose supernormal powers were perfected, whose noble wisdom was vast and pervasive, whose eloquence was unimpeded, whose samādhis were firmly established, and who were erudite in every field of knowledge.

At that time, there was a bodhisattva named Vimalagarbha who, together with ninety-two thousand bodhisattvas, traveled from the land of the Tathāgata Samantakusuma—whose world is named Viśuddhacaryā—to the Vulture Peak in the Sahā world.
The World-Honored One saw from afar the Bodhisattva Vimalagarbha, surrounded by a retinue of countless thousands of mahāsattvas, walking through the void. The Buddha thought to himself:

"This Vimalagarbha has traveled by various routes through distant lands to proclaim the command of the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Samantakusuma; he has come to receive this 'Universal Gateway' chapter and shall now assemble the multitude of bodhisattvas."

At that time, the Great Sage, manifesting his teachings and demonstrating his spiritual resonance exactly as they were, caused the bodhisattvas from countless and limitless worlds to arrive immediately; they came to this Sahā world and proceeded to Vulture Peak Mountain.
He proceeded to where the Buddha was, prostrated at his feet, and withdrew to stand to one side.
All the bodhisattvas dwelling on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa who were living in seclusion and tranquility also came to the assembly; having completed their salutations, they withdrew to sit down.

At that moment, the Bodhisattva Vimalagarbha miraculously manifested a lotus flower made of the seven precious substances, with a thousand petals; he took it and went to the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Śākyamuni, prostrated himself, and presented it to him.
Jie said:
"The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Puhua, the Holy Honored One of the Pure Conduct World, respectfully inquires after you with boundless concern:
'Are your movements vigorous and strong? Are your powers light and agile? Is your daily life peaceful and secure? Do you bring much relief and salvation to others?'"

"Now that you have been sent here, I respectfully approach you to receive and accept this inconceivable and pure chapter on the Universal Gate, which is for the sake of explaining it to the bodhisattvas.

At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Vimalagarbha exchanged greetings; having finished his salutations, he withdrew and sat cross-legged in mid-air together with the other bodhisattvas upon precious lotus flowers.
At that time, the youth Mañjuśrī rose from his seat in the assembly, adjusted his robes, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his hands joined in reverence, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Excellent, World-Honored One!
I pray that you will explain the source of the Dharma in the "Chapter on the Inconceivable Universal Gateway," analyzing and expounding it for the sake of all bodhisattvas!

Recall that in the distant past, long ago, from the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Samantamukha, I heard this sutra and gave rise to eighty-four trillion samādhis, and have long since attained the practice of seventy-seven trillion koṭis of dhāraṇī gates.
"I only pray, World-Honored One,
that out of compassion for all bodhisattvas, you will proclaim this once again.
The Buddha addressed the youth Prabhūtaratna:
"Listen attentively!
Reflect upon it well.
He replied:
"So be it, World-Honored One!
We wish and desire to hear.
Mañjuśrī and the various bodhisattvas received the instruction and listened.
The Buddha told Pu-shou:
"If there is a bodhisattva who wishes to study the dharmas entered through the Universal Gate, they should practice the equal-minded discernment that enters into form,
the equal-minded discernment that enters into sound, and the equal-minded discernment that enters into odor..."
The mental discrimination of fragrances and so forth; the mental discrimination of entering into various flavors and so forth;
the mental discrimination of entering into tactile sensations and so forth; the mental discrimination of entering into mental natures and so forth;
the mental discrimination of entering into women and so forth; the mental discrimination of entering into men and so forth; the mental discrimination of entering into young girls and so forth.
He enters into the mental discriminations of children and others; he enters into the mental discriminations of the devas and others; he enters into the mental discriminations of the nāgas and others;
he enters into the mental discriminations of the yakṣas and others; he enters into the mental discriminations of the gandharvas and others;
he enters into the mental discriminations of the asuras and others; he enters into the mental discriminations of the garuḍas and others.

Discriminating, they range through the mental discriminations of the Kinnaras and others; they range through the mental discriminations of the Mahoragas and others; they range through the mental discriminations of entering the hells and others;
they range through the mental discriminations of entering the realm of hungry ghosts and others; they range through the mental discriminations of entering the realm of animals and others;
they range through the mental discriminations of entering into lustful desire and others; they range through the mental discriminations of entering into anger...
They range through mental discriminations such as anger; they range through mental discriminations such as ignorance; they range through mental discriminations of various unwholesome states;
they range through mental discriminations of the roots of all virtues; they range through mental discriminations of all conditioned phenomena;
and they range through mental discriminations of all unconditioned phenomena.
"Samantabhadra!

Wherever bodhisattvas may travel, they are fully equipped for all things; they dwell in equanimity and are endowed with the ultimate Way. This is the method for training in and entering the Samādhi of the Universal Gate."
The Buddha addressed the youth Viśeṣacintin:
"What is meant by a bodhisattva entering into the discernment of form with an equanimous mind?
To understand form as being like a bubble on water—unobtainable, incapable of being maintained, and lacking solidity—is to observe with an equanimous mind that no such form exists."
"This is called the bodhisattva’s equanimous wandering within form.
He further addressed Puśya:
"What is meant by the bodhisattva’s equanimous mental discernment in entering sounds?"
It is like the sound of a person’s call, which elicits an echo; yet as soon as it arises, it immediately vanishes, leaving no form or image and nothing known of its origin.

All things are devoid of multiplicity and lack distinction, nor do they possess any marks. Having realized that there are no marks, one understands that what people speak of is empty and without reality. Once one has comprehended all sounds—just as an echo in the deep mountains responds to a call—one then contemplates them with equanimity;
this is called entering into all sounds through the contemplation of equality.
He further addressed Pṛthuśas:
"What is meant by the Bodhisattva’s equanimous mind discerning and entering into odors and fragrances?

For hundreds of billions of kalpas he travels back and forth, and though his nose smells them, he never grows weary; it is like the depths of the great ocean, which can never be filled. The image of these fragrances cannot be grasped, for they are deceptive phenomena lacking in ultimate truth. Even if one seeks their reality, there is no point of convergence; they are non-existent and cannot be maintained."

"The locus of the nose has no reality; it is as vague and empty as space, like a phantom created by illusion. Even if it were made distinct, there would be no equal contemplation through which one could enter into the smelling of odors.
He further addressed Pṛthuśas:
"What is meant by a bodhisattva’s equal-minded discernment in entering among various flavors?"

When it reaches the throat and pharynx, one does not perceive a salty taste, nor is there an absence of tasting; these distinctions arise from causes and conditions. That which the tongue finds sweet is likewise a convergence of conditions. When one clearly awakens to the state of non-conceptualization, one attains equal contemplation and enters into all flavors.
He further addressed Pṛthuśas:
“What is meant by a bodhisattva’s equanimous mind discerning and entering into fine and smooth sensations?
Regarding these fine and smooth sensations, the will has a point of attachment and seeks to obtain them through conditions; yet that which is soft and smooth cannot be obtained.”

Having already perceived these conditions, one finds that the subtle and smooth, as well as the coarse and rough, have no fixed place of abiding; when calculating the subtle and smooth, they are found to have no formation and nothing upon which they depend.
"Because one is attached to clothing, there is a basis for reliance; this is what is meant by 'equanimous contemplation' as one enters into fine textures.
He further addressed Puśya:
"What is meant by a bodhisattva’s equanimous mind that discriminates and enters into mental phenomena?"
Suppose all people of the three realms were gathered together and stationed in one place; though one sought their grasping minds, they could not be found.

No form or image was seen, nor was there any hesitation, nor any coming together or dispersing; their dwelling place was unknown. They manifested various colors, yet within, there was no location; that location had no fixed abode. Like a phantom created by a magician, it is empty and unreal; thus one should practice equal contemplation and enter into the mental phenomena.
He further addressed Pṛthuśas:
"What is meant by a bodhisattva entering among women with an impartial mind?
One observes that within the four great elements there is no woman; it is only those deluded by ignorance who are confused by craving and desire, becoming lost in the void."

To consider women is like a magician conjuring the image of a woman; following their conduct and according to what they enjoy, one gives rise to thoughts of sensual desire toward women who are like illusions.
They have no women; it is only the deluded who are confused by them.
One who can discern that all women are without marks, that they are equal in liberation, and that they manifest as female forms, thus regards them with equanimity and enters among women.
He further addressed Pṛthuśas:
"What is meant by a bodhisattva entering into the discernment of men with an impartial mind?

It is as if a man were to spontaneously resolve: 'I am a hero. He gives rise to the thought that this is a woman, yet his mind is free from desire and there is no substantiality to be obtained. He does not perceive the form of a woman; he contemplates all forms with equanimity and gives rise to the perception of them as women."
If one contemplates that these males and females are like a mirage or the moon reflected in water, then there are no males or females.

Realizing that the male has no form and exists as a mere deceptive construct, once one is able to attain equanimity, one can manifest as a female; thus, through equal contemplation, one enters into the state of a man.
He further addressed Puśya:
"What is meant by a bodhisattva entering the state of a youth with an impartial mind?
It is like a tree: if there are no sprouts, there will be no roots or trunk; if there are no roots or trunk, there will be no flowers or fruit; likewise, if there is no woman, there can be no youth."

Taking the name "Child" as the condition, one contemplates ignorance; awakening to the non-arising of the female, one finds no nature of a son. Understanding that all things are non-existent, one then enters the state of the Child through equal contemplation.
He further addressed Pṛthuśas:
"What is meant by a bodhisattva entering the state of a 'maiden' (*kumārikā*) through the equalization of mind and discernment?

It is like uprooting a tree so that its roots never grow again; the wise one does not seek fruit therein. To understand the meaning of ugliness and reach discernment, to awaken all forms of vigor and non-conceptuality, and to dry up the many streams—this is what constitutes a maiden."
“Having understood that a girl is thus, and that what is manifested is equal, one then enters the state of a young girl through impartial observation.
He further addressed Puśya:
“What is meant by a bodhisattva entering among the devas with an impartial mind and through discernment?”

The various heavens are adorned and purified; their merits are spontaneous, and their intentions are fresh and pure. Their palaces are exquisitely decorated, yet there is no one who constructed them. The wondrous flowers of the trees of mind have no one who planted their seeds. Their blessings are like illusory transformations, arising from inconceivable sources. Pure light flows forth, and they attain the purity of nirvana. They realize that the heavens are empty and false, established in a state of ethereal vacuity. Through supreme discourse on equality, they manifest the forms of the various heavens. This is the bodhisattva’s entry into and wandering among the heavens.
He further addressed Pṛthuśas: "What is it for a bodhisattva to enter among the various nāgas with an impartial mind?

Seeing that there is no seeking for birth, they raise clouds for seven days; the rain that falls moistens all things, yet it abides neither inside nor outside. It spreads throughout Jambudvīpa and gradually returns to the great ocean. As for the waters that fill [the earth], they originate from where they come; so too do sentient beings learn through various conditions, manifesting all kinds of sins and blessings. Yet, naturally, sentient beings are non-existent; only the ignorant take the void for reality. To perceive the nāgas as equal—this is what it means for a bodhisattva to travel impartially among the nāgas."
He further addressed Pǔshǒu:
"What is meant by 'the Bodhisattva’s impartial mind discerning and entering among ghosts and spirits'?
When the mind is like an open door, it possesses form and image; its body is tall and vast, and the mind constitutes a single category."

The mind should not be intimidated by difficulties, for fear arises from conditions. Seeing that phenomena have no reality and that all manifold perceptions cannot be conceptualized, one realizes that what lacks reality is emptiness. To preach the equality of quiescence while manifesting the form of a ghost—this is the bodhisattva’s equal wandering among ghosts and spirits.
He further addressed Pṛthuśas:
"What is meant by a bodhisattva entering the realm of the gandharvas with impartial intent?

Their dharma has no going, yet their voice speaks of going; they understand that there is neither coming nor going, and thus they speak of the gandharvas with equanimity. This is what is called a bodhisattva entering the realm of the gandharvas through impartial observation."
He further addressed Pṛthuśas:
“What is meant by a bodhisattva entering the realm of the asuras with an impartial mind through discernment?

It is not by means of causal conditions; rather, the minds of asuras are equal—without arising, without ceasing, and without birth—and thus they manifest equality. This is what is called a bodhisattva entering the realm of the asuras through impartial contemplation.”
He further addressed Pṛthuśas:
"What is meant by a bodhisattva entering the *garuḍa* realm with an impartial mind through discernment?

To construct and experience that which is without reception, to establish words and names, and to contemplate the *garuḍa* as being without name or form—this is called a bodhisattva entering the *garuḍa* realm."
He further addressed Pṛthuśas:
"What is meant by a bodhisattva entering the Cāturmahārājakāyika heaven with an impartial mind through discernment?

Since phenomena are unconditioned yet manifest as conditioned, one establishes the Cāturmahārājakāyika; since discernment is without arising, it is the equality of the Cāturmahārājakāyika. This is what is meant by a bodhisattva entering the Cāturmahārājakāyika through impartial contemplation."
He further addressed Pṛthuśas:
"What is meant by 'the Bodhisattva’s impartial mind discerning and entering Maheśvara'?

Regarding the designation of that dharma, he establishes various dharmas for persons, yet there is no characteristic therein; it is an empty discernment. All perceptions and non-perceptions naturally proclaim the sound of equality, manifesting Maheśvara. This is called the Bodhisattva’s impartial contemplation and entry into Maheśvara."
He further addressed Puśya: "What is meant by a bodhisattva’s equanimous mind that discerns and enters the hells?

The hells have no master; they are empty and without a creator. They arise from one's own perceptions, yet these perceptions do not truly arise. All hells are pure, fresh, and stainless. Wisdom-realization is like an illusion; fundamentally they are non-existent and signless. Being signless and non-existent, they are distinct like space. When the hells manifest with equal tranquility, this is called a bodhisattva’s equanimous wandering in the hells."
He further addressed Pṛthuśas:
"What is meant by a bodhisattva’s impartial mind that distinguishes and enters among the hungry ghosts?

Hungry ghosts have no form and no name; they originally have no dwelling place. One encounters them because of stinginess, yet stinginess has no abode. Not understanding that all things exist, one calculates in terms of 'self,' 'others,' and 'persons. Knowing that these are entirely without foundation and realizing there are no hungry ghosts—this is what it means for a bodhisattva to impartially roam among the hungry ghosts."
He further addressed Puśya: "What is meant by a bodhisattva’s impartial mind that distinguishes and enters the realm of animals?

Like clouds and mist, they manifest various colors, yet they have no fixed form and are entirely non-existent. Their mental activity is empty and void, equal to the density of fog; their various forms and images, as well as the dispositions of animals, are like illusions. Through delusion and falsehood, they speak of animal forms, yet they equally proclaim the sound of tranquility. This is called the bodhisattva’s impartial wandering among animals."
He further addressed Pǔshǒu: "What is meant by a bodhisattva’s equanimous mind discerning and entering into lust? Lust arises from conceptualization;

yet that which is conceptualized has no existence, no reality, no form, no appearance, and no abiding place—it cannot be found. Lust is like space. Delusion, inverted thoughts, and the defilements of affliction are such that dharmas have no dust or stain. Desire is empty like space; even if one were to seek it throughout the ten directions, it could not be seen. Lust has no shape; through the darkness of ignorance, greed, and fear, one finds no peace. There is no calamity, yet one harbors fear."
For example, it is like a man who, having nothing to grasp, conceives fear; terrified, he abandons everything and flees, yet he does not perceive that all is empty—everything is indeed empty.

He attains no liberation; through folly and inversion, he instead creates contrary conceptions. Shrouded in darkness and lacking understanding, he fails to see that dharmas are like space. The Buddhas of the past, future, and present have understood all greed and desire; yet there is no liberation from greed and desire, for the notion of craving is entirely empty. To revile lust while seeking liberation from desire—all this is without foundation, for its root is naturally pure.

Seeing the Buddha’s place of enlightenment as equal and free from conceptualization, and beholding all beings as such, one yearns for detachment from desire. Since that which is conceptualized is empty and precarious, one thereby leaves behind all thoughts. According to the aspiration thus aroused, one seeks liberation from greed and lust, intending to cross over the realm of desire.
To conceive of nothing sought, not to destroy the primordial limit (*koṭi*), and for desire to be without thought—such is original purity; thus, one does not conceive of liberation.

Even if one were to transcend desire, to regard that as purity would be a misconception; desire is empty and non-existent. To reckon this as dual is the mark of ignorance and darkness; when the practitioner deeply contemplates it as being like an illusion, they do not lose the essential point.

When various thoughts arise, no greed or desire is produced; though "love and desire" is a mere provisional designation, there is no attachment or clinging to names. All names are unimpeded, and one knows that desire cannot be attained. Beholding the truth and investigating emptiness, one harbors no greed or desire. Not perceiving liberation as something to be known, one regards greed and desire for the Buddha-dharma as equal to *nirvāṇa*. Understanding the aggregate of greed and desire, one is equally free from the notion of self. Knowing that greed and desire are quiescent, one maintains equanimity amidst tranquility and fear. Viewing the aggregate of desire as equal to an illusion or a transformation—this is the bodhisattva’s impartial engagement with lust.
He further addressed Pṛthuśas:
"What is meant by a bodhisattva’s impartial mind discerning and entering into anger?
Anger arises from opposition; opposition is born of causes and conditions. One who is without a self designates it as 'self,' thereby establishing immeasurable matters."
Just as when trees grow together, they produce a fierce and poisonous resentment; yet their sound is naturally empty, being without thought or existence.

Like trees dwelling in seclusion that rub against one another until fire ignites, when the conditions disperse, the fire is extinguished and no longer appears; the arising of emptiness is like this, and so too is the coarse sound.
Because one seeks to weigh and measure, anger does not arise.
It does not originate from sound, nor does it dwell within the body, nor does it come from without.
Since it arises through emptiness, originates from other conditions, and is established through opposition, when each is analyzed individually, there is no hatred.
Just as with the faults of the wind element, resentment arises from pride; yet if one understands skillful means, it establishes conditions through perception. Such is the case with foul sounds:

hatred arises from emptiness, and hatred in turn burns oneself, endangering one's own person. By distinguishing the thought of anger, one finds it ultimately devoid of form or image. Examining sound with equanimity and listening to the voice of anger, one realizes that the root of resentment is equal [to its opposite], having no origin and nothing to grasp. By discerning the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), one beholds equality; this is what is meant by a bodhisattva’s equanimous engagement with anger.
He further addressed Pṛthuśas:
"What is meant by a bodhisattva’s impartial mind discerning and entering into ignorance?

Ignorance arises from non-arising; one observes that ignorance does not exist. Since it is non-existent, there is no madness and no darkness of madness. A person has no obscuration, and their vows are unimpeded. Seeking the direction of emptiness, they realize that the cultivation of ignorance is itself void."
The conduct of the ignorant is the most difficult to master; they are shrouded in ignorance regarding all phenomena, taking mental constructions as defilements.
It is like a man who wishes to cross the void—he would not succeed even in ten million eons—yet he knows the beginning and end of the void; so too it is with the ignorant.

The fundamental limit is free from deluded discourse; obscured and dark, it does not give rise to defilement. There is nothing to be accomplished or fulfilled, like crossing through empty space where one cannot discern directions. Furthermore, there is no completeness and no one capable of traversing it, even over hundreds of thousands of kalpas. One who practices amidst the darkness of pleasure finds no satiety therein and is never satisfied.
It is like a child blowing air into a leather bag; as soon as he opens his mouth, one observes that there is nothing there at all.

Offenses and blessings are like this empty bag; yet through habitual ignorance, one seeks them and cannot find them. One harbors desires, claiming that ignorance is bottomless, but its roots are severed and it is formless; having no root and no dwelling place, it is therefore inexhaustible.
Even if one were to exhaust all foolishness, this [attainment] would still be unobtainable; for these sentient beings are like illusions and cannot be granted [such a state].
Even if one were to create a metaphor, such that one could deliver all classes of beings within the three realms every day and cause them to attain *nirvāṇa*— [This remains impossible.]
The Buddha’s lifespan remains in the world for incalculable billions of kalpas; he delivers and liberates the masses, yet the number of people can never be exhausted.
Because of ignorance, the seeds [of existence] are established; the realm of humanity is devoid of conceptual thought, and this deluded darkness is like an illusion—it is ungraspable.

The Buddha is equal to the fool; observing them, one sees they are non-dual. If one can observe with such equality, one is able to mind the Way. Folly and wisdom are one and the same, free from all obscurations and hindrances. Among the multitudes of sentient beings, there is no distinction between the foolish and the wise. Folly is incalculable; when one contemplates the traces of the mind, that mind is without conceptualization and has no boundaries. Since the darkness of folly is limitless, it cannot be grasped.
From where does the ignorance of one's disposition arise? Once delusion has ceased to arise, what kind of darkness remains?
Just as delusion has no location, so too is the Buddha-way; it is utterly without limit or depth, for all phenomena are non-dual.

The equality of distinct sounds is to equally examine the resonance of delusion; to realize that they are one and the same as emptiness, and that ignorance is like clouds; through the equality of such discernment, one then understands the concentrated mind.
"This is what it means for a bodhisattva to wander equally amidst ignorance.
He further addressed Pṛthuśas:
"What is meant by a bodhisattva’s equal-minded discernment that enters into non-virtue?"

He practices desirelessness without form, practices non-anger without location, and does not practice delusion; he knows the equality of all beings, that all defilements are entirely level, that he has attained liberation into emptiness, and that all that exists is understood as pure.
"In this way, it is said that the bodhisattva enters into all unwholesome states with an impartial mind.
He then addressed Puśya:
"What is meant by the bodhisattva entering into all roots of wholesome virtue with an impartial mind?"

Sentient beings cultivate goodness with various mental activities; yet all these activities are but a single practice, always understood as equal. Having realized this equality, one sees that all practices are like illusions and that distinct sounds are of one essence; thus, one understands the nature of speech and sound.
"This is what it means for a bodhisattva to roam equally amidst all virtues.
He further addressed Pu-shou:
"What is meant by a bodhisattva roaming with an equanimous mind to enter into and discern conditioned phenomena?"

All things are non-existent; they are incalculable, immeasurable, and difficult to reckon. They are always understood as equal, comprehended as infinite, without activity and without form. They are liberated and equally tranquil; one beholds all things as peaceful.
"This is what it means for a bodhisattva to wander equally amidst the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
He then addressed Puśya:
"What is meant by a bodhisattva who, with an equanimous mind, discerns and enters into the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*)?"

The dharmas are fundamentally pure and quiescent, and there is no meeting or assembly therein. Ignorance is a mere provisional sound; one should equally examine all sounds as being without words and without instruction, fully realizing them to be unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). One should thus contemplate with equanimity all attachments to words and sounds.
"This is what it means for a bodhisattva to roam equally within the unconditioned.
He further addressed Puśya:
"What is meant by a bodhisattva roaming in equanimity with an equalized mind through discernment?"
Not dwelling in the conditioned, nor abiding in the unconditioned, all formations are equal, like space, without obstruction.
The three realms have no fundamental basis; what, then, is sought in nirvana?
Neither emerging nor entering, even unto great peace, it delivers sentient beings; it resolves that there are no diversities, for the Dharma-body is like space—neither conjoined nor dispersed.
"This is what it means for a bodhisattva to roam equally within equality.
When the World-Honored One spoke these verses and phrases, they were timely and inconceivable.

Ninety-nine thousand bodhisattvas attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas; seventy-two billion hundred-thousand devas and humans all resolved their minds upon the unsurpassed, right, and true path; three million six hundred thousand bhikṣus exhausted their outflows and attained liberation of mind; and six thousand bhikṣuṇīs all resolved their minds upon the unsurpassed, right, and true path.
Two thousand two hundred laymen of pure faith and one thousand eight hundred laywomen of pure faith all resolved their minds upon the unsurpassed, right, and true path.
At that time, the youth Mañjuśrī addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"I pray only that the Great Sage..."
The Bodhisattva manifests the name of this samādhi and thereby attains supreme virtue, with all faculties becoming clear and lucid.

Upon hearing the name by which this samādhi is caused, one shall obtain illumination regarding all dharmas such that nothing remains unpenetrated, and shall completely subdue all multitudes of deluded beings and those with false views.

Delighting in a single syllable, they discern and understand all syllables; by means of all syllables, they realize the single syllable. Their wisdom of eloquence is immeasurable as they expound the Dharma for the sake of all sentient beings. They discern and understand the patience regarding the dharma of conditional response, entering into the single characteristic through all practices. Having attained infinite and boundless meanings, they thoroughly understand the meaning of consciousness and the four analytical eloquences.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One addressed the youth Viśeṣacintin:
“Listen attentively!
Reflect upon this well!”
"I shall now analyze the beginning and end for you,
O Benevolent One. He replied, "Excellent!"
"I wish to hear it with joy.
The Buddha said:
"There is a samādhi named 'Detachment from Immeasurable Defilements. If a bodhisattva attains this concentration, they will universally perceive all forms as pure."
The Buddha told Puśya:
"There is a samādhi named 'Embracing Diversity. If a bodhisattva attains this concentration, the radiance of their wisdom will outshine the light of all the suns and moons."

There is a samādhi named "Perfectly Accomplished Radiance. If a bodhisattva attains this concentration, its majestic brilliance eclipses that of Śakra and Brahmā; the darkness of the three realms is entirely dispelled and granted peace, while the splendors of the various devas suddenly cease to appear.

There is a samādhi called "Abandoning the Elements" (*dhātuparityāga*); if a bodhisattva attains this concentration, they eliminate all maladies of lust, anger, and delusion while dwelling amidst the assembly.
There is a samādhi called "Unassailable" (*anabhibhūta*); if a bodhisattva attains this concentration, they illuminate all Buddha-fields throughout the eight directions, above, and below.

There is a samādhi named "The Non-arising of All Dharmas. If a bodhisattva attains this concentration, they will master the scriptures, discourses, and treatises of all Buddhas, and expound them in detail for the sake of the assembly.
There is a samādhi called "Mindfulness of the Sound of Thunder. If a bodhisattva attains this concentration, their speech and voice will extend as far as the Brahma-heaven.

There is a samādhi called "Illuminating All That Is Desired by the Minds of Sentient Beings. If a bodhisattva attains this concentration, they will gladden sentient beings and cause them to attain liberation according to whatever they desire.

There is a samādhi named "Manifesting Joy through Unconverging Diligence. If a bodhisattva attains this concentration, they directly perceive the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta), which is without limit or number; they thoroughly penetrate all that is heard and seen, including the delusions regarding beginning and end.

There is a samādhi named "Treasure Virtue Delighting in the World of Non-conceptuality. If a bodhisattva attains this concentration, they will manifest various supernatural powers to transform and guide sentient beings.

There is a samādhi called "Convergence of All Sounds. If a bodhisattva attains this concentration, they awaken to all speech and sounds; by means of non-dual numbers, they comprehend a single syllable, and with a single syllable, they expound non-dual numbers.

There is a samādhi named "Accumulating All Meritorious Virtues. If a bodhisattva attains this concentration, they will discern offenses and blessings while manifesting equanimity, bringing great joy to all sentient beings.

They then hear the voice of the Buddha, the voice of the Dharma, and the voices of the assembly—the voices of śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas, as well as the voices of the perfections (pāramitās); yet, that which they speak is itself devoid of sound.
There is a samādhi named "The Arising of All Dhāraṇīs as the King of All," by which, if a bodhisattva attains this concentration, they can discern all immeasurable dhāraṇīs.

There is a samādhi called "Purifying All Eloquence. If a bodhisattva attains this concentration, all sounds and speech are stilled and eliminated; there is neither verbal instruction nor responsive resonance, and being without speech or instruction, there is nothing at all.
Thereupon, Puśya addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"Indeed, Great Sage!
May this humble self be permitted to expound upon the merit of this sutra?"
He said, "You should expound it.
Puśya addressed the Buddha:

"If a bodhisattva hears this sutra and does not harbor doubt, but resolves to accept, uphold, recite, and read it, that person will in the present life attain wondrous eloquence: eloquence of intelligence, eloquence of joy, eloquence of profound subtlety, and eloquence that is never obstructed. They shall constantly practice a mind of loving-kindness toward all sentient beings, harboring no intent to harm."
"Why is this? Even if one were to contemplate what has been done and where one is headed, by practicing the truth of wisdom, it shall never be abandoned from one's person.
At that time, the World-Honored One praised Pu-shou (Mañjuśrī), saying:
“Excellent, excellent!
You have spoken these words most skillfully; they are indeed as you intend.
It is, for example, like practicing generosity to attain great wealth, which is never in vain.”
Observing the precepts leads to rebirth in the heavens without falsehood;
likewise, this present sutra is also thus: by studying it, one attains eloquence without it being established in vain, and fully realizes one's original aspiration.
Just as when the sun rises and shines upon the world, all darkness is dispelled, so it is with this sutra: those who recite and study it will possess eloquence and attain thorough understanding.
It is like a bodhisattva sitting at the site of enlightenment beneath the Bodhi tree, attaining the unsurpassed, true, and correct path and achieving supreme perfect awakening;
likewise, a bodhisattva who studies and recites this sutra will surely obtain eloquence and eliminate all doubts.
Therefore, Puṣya!

If a bodhisattva wishes to manifest eloquence and become thoroughly proficient in all dharmas, upon hearing this sutra, their mind shall not hesitate; they should immediately receive, uphold, expound, recite, and extensively explain its meaning for the sake of the assembled multitude.
Thereupon, the Bodhisattva Vimalagarbha came forward and addressed the Buddha:

“After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, should there be those who receive, uphold, recite, and expound this sutra-dharma, and who extensively elucidate its meaning for the great assembly—I, your humble servant, shall become a refuge for those of little understanding, causing them to be free from doubt and to swiftly attain eloquence.”
At that time, the evil Māra, distressed and weeping, approached the Buddha and said to the World-Honored One:
"May this sutra never be established!"
The Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, constantly harbors great compassion; to those who suffer and are afflicted, he bestows great peace.
How excellent, O Great Sage! I pray that you remove my distress.

Just as in the past when the World-Honored One first sat beneath the tree at the site of enlightenment, may you now once again expound this sutra. My current grief and mental anguish are even greater than when the Tathāgata first attained the Way of the Buddha. At such a time of seeking salvation, my tossing and turning cannot be overcome.

All shall attain the stage of non-retrogression, reach the unsurpassed, true, and correct path, and achieve supreme perfect enlightenment. Any sentient beings who merely hear this sutra, or who bow their heads upon hearing its name, shall all attain the Way and reach nirvana; they shall empty my realm and leave the palaces of Māra desolate.
"The Great Sage nurtures and dwells in peace, bestowing tranquility; he has raised up great compassion and looks only upon us with pity and salvation.
The Buddha said to Māra: "Pāpīyan!..."
"Do not be afraid; do not harbor fear. It is not that all sentient beings have not yet attained parinirvāṇa, nor is it that the Tathāgata has not established this sutra.
When Māra heard the Buddha’s words, he leaped for joy with great delight; a wholesome mind arose within him, and he suddenly vanished.
Puśya addressed the Buddha, saying,
"For what reason do you preach the teaching of severance for the sake of Māra?
The Buddha told Puśya:
"This sutra abides in non-abiding; therefore, Māra speaks these words:
'I do not establish this sutra!'"
This is most sincere and not false. All dharmas abide in non-abiding;

they cannot be grasped, they are beyond verbal instruction, and they are free from duality. Their primordial limit is equal, being fundamentally without origin. The Dharma-realm is like a scale, as level as empty space; it has no preference and no aversion, being truly and perfectly without distinction.
"Now that this sutra circulates throughout Jambudvīpa, there shall be auspicious omens here in this world.

As soon as the World-Honored One established this teaching of absolute truth, a voice spontaneously resounded from the air, heard everywhere: "It is exactly as the Buddha has said; it is true and not false."
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"Receive this essential sūtra, the 'Universal Gate Chapter,' and uphold, recite, read, and proclaim it to your fellow students.
He further said to Ānanda:
“The treasury of eighty-four thousand dharma-doors, when compared to this sutra, is equal and without distinction. Why is this so?

Because the immeasurable gates and essential points of the Dharma-realm are fully discerned and understood by the Tathāgata; it is through understanding this sutra that sentient beings achieve the Buddha-way, and only thereafter does he preach the eighty-four thousand treasuries of various sūtra-doors.”
"Therefore, Ānanda!
You should receive this sutra, grasp its message, and in accordance with the truth, uphold, recite, and explain it for the sake of all people.

When the Buddha had finished speaking these words, the Bodhisattva Vimalagarbha, the youth Mañjuśrī, the venerable Ānanda, and the devas, humans, gandharvas, and asuras, having heard the sutra, rejoiced, prostrated themselves, and withdrew.
The Sutra on the Universal Gate Chapter Spoken by the Buddha
